subject: ela
intro: In each item below you will read two longer informational texts about the same event or person. One is usually a firsthand account (a memoir or first-person account written by someone who was there), and the other is an outside account (a biography, profile, or report written by an observer). The two accounts agree on the basic facts but often differ in what they emphasize, how they interpret events, and the conclusions they draw. Read both carefully, then answer the question. Each answer asks you to evaluate or synthesize across both texts, so support your thinking with evidence from both.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of the 1937 launch of the lifeboat from the sinking trawler Greenshank, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from the memoir of Tom Hale, a deckhand who was aboard):
I was nineteen, and I had never been so cold. The Greenshank had been taking water for an hour before the captain finally gave the order to lower the boat. My hands would not close around the rope the way I told them to. The sea kept slamming the lifeboat against the hull, and twice I was sure it would splinter. What I remember most is the silence among us. Nobody shouted. We were too frightened to shout. When the captain said to row, I rowed, but I could not feel the oar. I only knew we were moving away because the dark shape of the ship grew smaller behind us. I thought of my mother. I thought we would all drown. By the time the rescue cutter found us at dawn, I had stopped believing morning would come. People say we were brave that night. I do not remember bravery. I remember being a boy who did exactly what he was told because he was too afraid to do anything else.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from a maritime history of North Sea rescues):
The Greenshank began taking on water at approximately 9 p.m. on November 3, 1937, after striking submerged wreckage. Captain Reed ordered the single lifeboat lowered at 10:14 p.m., once the pumps could no longer keep pace. All eleven crewmen, including the deckhand Tom Hale, boarded successfully despite a heavy swell. The crew rowed clear of the foundering vessel and maintained their position through the night. At 6:40 a.m. the following morning, the rescue cutter Aldgate located the lifeboat and recovered all hands. No lives were lost. The incident is frequently cited as a model of disciplined crew conduct, and Captain Reed was later commended for the timing of his evacuation order.

QUESTION: A student says the two authors disagree about what happened that night. Explain why this judgment is wrong, and describe more accurately how the two accounts relate to each other. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: The judgment is wrong because the two authors do not disagree on a single fact. Both report that the Greenshank took on water, that the lifeboat was lowered, that all the crew got clear of the ship and rowed away, that they waited through the night, and that a rescue cutter found them at dawn with no lives lost. The history states 'No lives were lost' and Hale describes the same rescue 'at dawn.' The accounts do not contradict; they cover the same event at different depths. The history reports the outside facts (times, names, the official commendation), while Hale's memoir reports the inside experience of those same events (the cold, the silence, his fear, his certainty they would drown). Rather than disagreeing, the firsthand account fills in the human feeling that the factual report leaves out, so together they give a fuller picture of one night that both agree happened.

steps: Check each text for the basic facts and compare them: ship taking water, lifeboat lowered, crew gets clear, waits all night, rescued at dawn, no deaths. Both texts report all of these.
Notice there is no fact one author asserts that the other denies, so 'disagree about what happened' is the wrong relationship.
Name the misconception: assuming two accounts of one event must contradict, when one is simply more detailed or differently focused than the other.

Describe the true relationship: the history gives the outside facts (10:14 p.m., Captain Reed, commendation) and the memoir gives the inside experience of the same events (the cold, the silence, the fear).

Support with evidence: history says 'all eleven crewmen... boarded successfully' and 'No lives were lost'; Hale describes that same escape from the inside, 'the dark shape of the ship grew smaller behind us.'
Conclude that the accounts complement rather than contradict each other, each supplying what the other omits about a single shared event.

Show the two are compatible: following orders exactly out of fear still looks orderly from outside, so both statements can describe the same behavior.

Connect each view to the author's relationship to the event: the historian works from records and an outside vantage, Hale from lived experience.
Conclude that the descriptions do not conflict; each captures a layer of the same event that the other author's position kept hidden.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of the first crossing of the Halden Pass by mountaineer Greta Voss, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from Voss's journal):
The storm came up faster than any of us guessed it would. We had planned to reach the saddle by noon, but by eleven the snow was blowing sideways and I could not see the rope to the climber ahead of me. My instinct was to push on. The summit was so close. But I stopped. I made everyone sit down in the lee of a boulder and wait. The others were angry. Anders argued with me for ten minutes. I held firm, though I will admit I was not certain I was right. We sat for three hours. When the storm broke, we climbed the last stretch in clear light and stood on the saddle at dusk. I have been praised for that decision ever since. The truth is I did not know it was the correct one. I only knew I was too afraid of the whiteout to move, and fear, that day, happened to point the same direction as wisdom.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from a profile of Voss in a climbing magazine):
Greta Voss is best known for her 1962 first crossing of the treacherous Halden Pass. When a sudden whiteout struck the team near the saddle, Voss made the decision that would define her reputation: she ordered the party to halt and shelter rather than risk the final ascent in zero visibility. Her teammates initially resisted, but Voss's calm authority prevailed. The team waited out the storm and completed the crossing safely at dusk. Mountaineering instructors still teach the episode as a textbook example of disciplined judgment under pressure, and Voss herself became a sought-after lecturer on decision-making in the mountains.

QUESTION: The magazine profile presents Voss's halt as an act of disciplined judgment. Voss's own journal presents it differently. Explain how the two accounts give a reader a different impression of why Voss stopped, and how each author's point of view leads to that difference. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: The profile leaves a reader thinking Voss stopped because she calmly judged it the wise thing to do; it calls the halt 'the decision that would define her reputation' and credits her 'calm authority' and 'disciplined judgment under pressure.' Voss's journal gives the opposite impression of her motive: she says 'I was not certain I was right' and admits 'I was too afraid of the whiteout to move, and fear, that day, happened to point the same direction as wisdom.' So the profile makes the halt look like deliberate good judgment, while the journal makes it look like fear that happened to be correct. The difference comes from point of view. The magazine writer is an outside observer judging Voss by the result, which was a safe crossing, so the outcome makes the decision look wise. Voss, writing from inside her own mind, knows the feeling that actually drove her and reports the doubt and fear the outside writer could not see.

steps: State the impression each text gives of Voss's reason for stopping. Profile: cool, deliberate judgment. Journal: fear she was not sure was correct.
Quote the profile's framing: 'calm authority' and 'a textbook example of disciplined judgment under pressure.'
Quote Voss's framing: 'I was too afraid of the whiteout to move, and fear, that day, happened to point the same direction as wisdom.'
Explain the source of the difference: the profile writer is outside and judges by the safe outcome, so the decision looks wise in hindsight.
Explain Voss's vantage: she writes from inside her own experience and can report the doubt and fear the observer cannot see.
Conclude that the same action gets two impressions because one author reads it from the result and the other from the lived motive.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of the night the town of Marsh Hollow was evacuated during the 1955 flood, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from a letter written by resident Ada Pell two weeks after the flood):
They knocked on our door near midnight and told us we had twenty minutes. I grabbed the children, the photographs, and the dog, and nothing else. We walked the three miles to the high school in the dark, and the water was already coming up over the road behind us. I keep hearing the people say afterward that the warning system worked, that everyone got out in time. Everyone in my family did, yes. But I want it remembered that the Coyle family on the river road got no knock at all. They climbed onto their roof and waited until morning for a boat. The word everyone is doing a lot of work in those reports, and I do not think it should.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from a county government report on the flood response):
On the night of April 9, 1955, rising water on the Marsh River triggered the county's emergency evacuation plan. Volunteers and sheriff's deputies went door to door beginning at 11:40 p.m., reaching the majority of low-lying homes within the hour. An estimated 600 residents were directed to the high school, which served as the emergency shelter. The evacuation is regarded as a success: no fatalities occurred, and the shelter operated without incident until residents were permitted to return three days later. The report notes that the door-to-door system reached most affected households in time for an orderly departure.

QUESTION: Both texts say no one died and the shelter worked, yet they leave a reader with different impressions of how well the evacuation went. Explain how the two accounts diverge in their interpretation of the same event, and how each author's purpose helps explain that divergence. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: The two accounts agree on the facts (no deaths, the shelter ran smoothly) but interpret the evacuation differently. The county report calls it 'a success' and stresses that the system 'reached most affected households in time,' leaving the impression that the plan worked well. Ada Pell, who lived through it, interprets the same night as a success with a serious gap: she points out that the Coyle family 'got no knock at all' and had to wait on their roof until morning, and she objects that the word 'everyone' in the reports 'is doing a lot of work.' Her impression is that the evacuation worked for most but failed some. The divergence follows from purpose. The county report is an official document evaluating its own emergency plan, so it emphasizes the overall success and the favorable statistic of 'most' households reached. Ada's letter is a personal account meant to make sure a forgotten family is remembered, so she emphasizes the exception the report rounds away.

steps: Confirm the shared facts both accept: no fatalities and the shelter operated without incident.
State the differing interpretations: the report calls it 'a success' that 'reached most affected households'; Ada sees a success with a real failure for the Coyles.
Quote the divergence: report says 'most affected households in time'; Ada says the Coyles 'got no knock at all' and that 'everyone... is doing a lot of work.'
Connect the report's purpose to its emphasis: as an official evaluation of the county's own plan, it highlights overall success and the word 'most.'
Connect Ada's purpose to her emphasis: as a resident wanting a forgotten family remembered, she highlights the exception the report's 'most' hides.
Conclude that identical facts yield different impressions because each author's purpose decides which facts to stress.

Explain the report-only reader's incomplete picture: 'most' and 'success' suggest the plan worked for everyone, hiding the missed family.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of inventor Lila Okafor's first public demonstration of her water filter, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from Okafor's memoir):
The newspapers wrote that the demonstration was a triumph. I have learned to smile when people say so. What actually happened is that the filter clogged after four minutes, and the clean water I poured for the mayor came from a backup jug I had hidden under the table. I had tested the device forty times in my workshop and it had worked thirty-nine. The fortieth time was the one that mattered, and it failed. I do not tell this story to diminish what came later. The filter I sell now is a good machine. But the version I showed that afternoon was not ready, and I knew it was not ready, and I let the room believe otherwise because I was desperate for the funding the mayor controlled. The triumph was real in its results. It was not honest in its origins.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from a biography of Okafor):
Okafor's public reputation was built in a single afternoon. At the 1991 civic fair, she demonstrated her low-cost water filter before the mayor and a crowd of onlookers, pouring a glass of purified water that, by all newspaper accounts, impressed the officials present. The demonstration secured the municipal grant that allowed her to refine the device, and within three years her filters were distributed across the region. The biographer notes that Okafor's later success vindicated the early confidence the demonstration inspired, and that the filter became one of the most widely adopted designs of its kind.

QUESTION: The biography treats the demonstration as a genuine triumph. The memoir reveals something the biography does not report. Explain what the memoir adds that changes how a reader understands that afternoon, and explain why the biographer, writing from outside, may not have known it. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: The memoir adds that the demonstration was secretly faked: the filter 'clogged after four minutes,' and the clean water Okafor poured for the mayor 'came from a backup jug I had hidden under the table.' The biography never reports this; it says the device 'impressed the officials present' and treats the day as a real triumph. This changes how a reader understands the afternoon completely. Instead of a working invention proving itself, the event becomes a desperate act of staging by an inventor who 'knew it was not ready' but needed the mayor's funding. The biographer may not have known this because, writing from outside, the biographer relied on what could be observed and recorded, chiefly 'newspaper accounts' of a successful demonstration. The hidden jug and the four-minute clog were private knowledge that only Okafor possessed; no outside observer in that room saw behind the table, so only her firsthand memoir could reveal it.

steps: Find the memoir's revelation: the filter 'clogged after four minutes' and the clean water 'came from a backup jug I had hidden under the table.'
Confirm the biography omits this; it relies on 'newspaper accounts' and calls the demonstration impressive.
Explain the change in understanding: a genuine success becomes a staged one, performed by someone who 'knew it was not ready.'
Explain the biographer's blind spot: as an outside observer working from public records, the biographer could only know what was visible and reported.
Note that the deception was private to Okafor, so only a firsthand source could expose it.
Conclude that the memoir's inside knowledge corrects the impression the outside account, through no fault of method, was bound to give.

QUESTION: A historian is writing about whether Okafor's 1991 filter actually worked at the demonstration. Judge which of these two accounts the historian should trust more for that specific question, and explain your reasoning using evidence from both texts. Be sure to address why the more reliable account is not simply the more recent or more official one.
items.answer: For the narrow question of whether the filter actually worked that day, the historian should trust the memoir. Okafor was in the room and behind the table, and she states plainly that the filter 'clogged after four minutes' and that the clean water 'came from a backup jug I had hidden under the table.' That is direct, firsthand knowledge of what the device did. The biography is not reliable on this point because its claim that the demonstration 'impressed the officials present' rests on 'newspaper accounts,' which recorded only the staged result and could not see the hidden jug. Importantly, the memoir is not more trustworthy here simply because it is more recent or because the biography is less official. It is more trustworthy because of the author's position: Okafor witnessed the failure firsthand, while the biographer and the newspapers witnessed only the appearance. On other questions, such as the filter's later success, the biography's outside view ('within three years her filters were distributed across the region') is perfectly sound. Reliability depends on who could actually see the thing being asked about.

Match the question to the source with direct access. Okafor was behind the table and saw the device clog.
Quote the firsthand evidence: 'clogged after four minutes' and the water 'came from a backup jug I had hidden under the table.'
Show why the biography is weak on this point: its claim rests on 'newspaper accounts' that saw only the staged result.
Address the trap directly: the memoir wins not because it is newer or the biography is unofficial, but because of the author's firsthand position.
Concede the biography's strength elsewhere ('within three years her filters were distributed') to show reliability depends on the specific question.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of the 1969 sit-in at Brearly College's administration building, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from the memoir of student organizer Renee Sato):
The newspapers called us a movement of two hundred. On the first night there were nine of us. I remember because I counted, over and over, lying on the cold marble floor of the dean's outer office, wondering if anyone would come in the morning. They did. By the third day the hall was full, and by the end of the week we did number in the hundreds. But I will never let anyone tell me it began as a flood. It began as a trickle, as nine frightened people who were not at all sure they would not be expelled and forgotten. The size came later. What we had at the start was not numbers. It was only the refusal of nine people to go home.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from a college history of campus protests):
The 1969 Brearly sit-in is remembered as one of the largest student demonstrations in the college's history. Beginning on a Monday in March, students occupied the administration building to demand reforms to the disciplinary code. The protest grew rapidly, drawing hundreds of participants within a week and attracting regional press coverage. After nine days, the administration agreed to negotiate, and several of the students' demands were eventually adopted. The episode is regarded as a turning point in the college's governance, demonstrating the capacity of organized students to influence institutional policy.

QUESTION: The college history emphasizes the protest's size and impact. Sato emphasizes its small and uncertain beginning. Explain how the difference in each author's point of view and purpose leads to a different overall impression of the sit-in, and explain what a reader understands by holding both impressions together. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: The college history leaves the impression of a large, confident movement: it remembers the sit-in as 'one of the largest student demonstrations in the college's history,' notes it 'grew rapidly, drawing hundreds,' and calls it 'a turning point in the college's governance.' Sato leaves the opposite impression of how it began: 'On the first night there were nine of us,' lying on a cold floor, 'not at all sure they would not be expelled,' with 'a trickle, not a flood.' The difference comes from point of view and purpose. The history is written by an outside institution looking back at the finished outcome, so it naturally measures the event by its peak size and lasting effect. Sato was one of the original nine and writes to honor the courage of that frightened start, so she measures the event by where it came from. Holding both together, a reader understands that a movement remembered as large and powerful actually grew out of the stubbornness of a tiny, scared group, so the impressive ending and the humble, brave beginning are two true parts of one story.

steps: State the history's impression and evidence: a large, influential protest, 'one of the largest... in the college's history,' 'a turning point.'
State Sato's impression and evidence: a tiny, frightened start, 'On the first night there were nine of us,' 'a trickle, not a flood.'
Tie the history's view to its point of view and purpose: an institution looking back, measuring by peak size and lasting effect.
Tie Sato's view to hers: a founding participant writing to honor the courage of the small beginning.
Synthesize: a movement remembered as large grew from the stubbornness of nine scared people.
Conclude that both impressions are true layers of one event, and a reader needs both to grasp it whole.

For the history, the hundreds are the headline, proof that this was 'one of the largest student demonstrations in the college's history' and evidence of the students' power to change policy. Show Sato's use of the same fact: as the 'later' contrast to the small start, 'The size came later.'
Link the history's use to its purpose: to record the event's institutional importance.
Link Sato's use to hers: to keep the brave nine from being erased, 'I will never let anyone tell me it began as a flood.'

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of polar explorer Henrik Dahl's 1911 return from the ice, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from Dahl's diary, written on the ship home):
They will want a hero when we dock, and I do not know how to be one. We did not reach the pole. We turned back forty miles short because Olsen's feet were frozen black and I judged he would lose them, or his life, if we went on. I made the choice alone, in the night, and I have not stopped questioning it. Perhaps a braver man would have pushed the last forty miles and claimed the prize. Perhaps a wiser one would have turned back sooner. I only know that Olsen walked off this expedition on his own two feet, and that the pole is still there, unreached, and that both of those facts are mine to carry. I am not sure which one the world will choose to remember me by.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from an encyclopedia entry on Dahl):
Henrik Dahl (1879 to 1948) was a Norwegian polar explorer best known for his 1911 expedition, which turned back approximately forty miles from the geographic pole. Although Dahl did not complete the journey, his decision to abort the final push is widely credited with saving the life of his companion, Lars Olsen, who was suffering from severe frostbite. Dahl was later honored not for reaching the pole, which he did not, but for the judgment and restraint he showed in withdrawing. He is frequently held up as an example of an explorer who valued the safety of his men above personal glory.

QUESTION: The encyclopedia presents Dahl's turning back as a clear, admirable act of judgment. Dahl's own diary presents the same decision with far more doubt. Explain how the firsthand and outside positions of the two authors produce this difference, and explain which account better captures Dahl's state of mind at the time and why. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: The encyclopedia, written from outside and after the fact, presents the turning back as settled, admirable judgment: it credits Dahl with 'the judgment and restraint he showed in withdrawing' and calls him an explorer 'who valued the safety of his men above personal glory.' Dahl's diary, written firsthand on the way home, is full of doubt: 'I have not stopped questioning it,' he wonders whether 'a braver man would have pushed' or 'a wiser one would have turned back sooner,' and he is unsure 'which one the world will choose to remember me by.' The difference grows out of position. The encyclopedist looks back on a known outcome (Olsen survived) and so can present the decision as clearly right. Dahl, living inside the moment with no idea how it would be judged, feels only the uncertainty of a hard choice. For Dahl's state of mind at the time, the diary is far better, because it was written then, by him, and records the questioning the calm outside summary completely smooths away.

steps: Capture the encyclopedia's framing: confident praise, 'the judgment and restraint he showed in withdrawing.'
Capture the diary's framing: doubt, 'I have not stopped questioning it,' unsure if a braver or wiser man would have chosen differently.
Explain the outside author's certainty: writing after the fact with a known outcome, Olsen survived, so the choice looks plainly right.
Explain the insider's doubt: living the moment with no idea how it would be judged.
Choose the better source for his state of mind: the diary, written then and by him.
Justify the choice with the contrast between 'I have not stopped questioning it' and the encyclopedia's settled praise.

items.answer: The encyclopedia can call the decision admirable judgment because it was written decades later by an outside observer who already knew how everything turned out. By then it was clear that Olsen survived, so the encyclopedist can confidently say the choice 'is widely credited with saving the life of his companion' and praise Dahl's 'judgment and restraint.' Dahl, writing 'on the ship home' the same week, could not say any of this, because he did not yet know how the choice would be judged: he opens 'They will want a hero when we dock, and I do not know how to be one,' and he was still living with the doubt, 'I have not stopped questioning it,' weighing whether 'a braver man would have pushed the last forty miles' or 'a wiser one would have turned back sooner.' The difference in timing explains the difference in confidence (hindsight turns a fearful gamble into obvious wisdom), and the difference in author explains the difference in feeling (the outsider reports a public verdict, while Dahl reports the inner uncertainty only the person making the choice could feel).

Explain the timing effect: the encyclopedist knew Olsen lived, so the choice looks 'widely credited with saving the life of his companion.'
Explain Dahl's lack of hindsight: he 'has not stopped questioning it' and does not know how he will be remembered.
Explain the authorship effect: an outsider can only report a public verdict; Dahl can report inner feeling.
Pair the evidence: encyclopedia's 'judgment and restraint' against Dahl's 'I have not stopped questioning it' and 'I do not know how to be' a hero.
Conclude that hindsight produces confidence and firsthand position produces the recorded doubt.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of the day pilot Mara Quinn landed a crippled airliner in a river in 2004, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from Quinn's later interview, transcribed):
People ask what I was thinking when both engines failed, as if I sat there reasoning it out. I was not reasoning. Training took over and I became, for about ninety seconds, a set of hands following a checklist I had practiced a thousand times. I did not feel calm. I felt nothing at all, which I have since learned is its own kind of terror. The part nobody asks about is afterward, standing on the wing in the cold water, counting passengers as they came out, and the long count where I was not sure the number would come out right. That was the moment I nearly came apart. The landing was the easy part. It was the counting that I still dream about.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from a federal aviation safety report):
On January 15, 2004, Flight 290 experienced dual engine failure shortly after takeoff following a bird strike. The captain, M. Quinn, executed a controlled ditching in the river within ninety seconds of the failure. All 154 occupants survived. The report attributes the successful outcome to the captain's adherence to established emergency procedures and to the rapid response of nearby vessels. Investigators concluded that the crew's actions were consistent with their training and that the decision to ditch, rather than attempt a return to the airport, was sound given the altitude and glide distance available.

QUESTION: The safety report and Quinn's interview both describe the same ninety seconds, yet each treats a different moment as the most important part of the event. Identify what each author treats as most important, and explain how each author's purpose accounts for that choice. Then explain what reading both together tells a reader about the event that neither gives alone. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: For the safety report, the most important part is the ditching itself, the technical decision and procedure. It centers on the captain's 'adherence to established emergency procedures' and the conclusion that 'the decision to ditch... was sound.' For Quinn, the landing is almost an afterthought ('The landing was the easy part'); the moment that matters to her is afterward, 'standing on the wing in the cold water, counting passengers,' the 'long count' where she 'nearly came apart.' Each choice follows from purpose. The report's job is to evaluate flight safety and procedure, so it focuses on the airmanship and ignores the counting on the wing, which is irrelevant to that goal. Quinn is telling her human experience, so the moment of greatest emotional weight is the most important to her. Reading both together tells a reader something neither gives alone: that a flawlessly executed, by-the-book emergency landing was, for the person who flew it, not the hardest part at all, so the event was at once a technical success and a private ordeal that the official record cannot show.

steps: Identify the report's focus: the ditching and procedure, 'adherence to established emergency procedures,' 'the decision to ditch... was sound.'
Identify Quinn's focus: the aftermath, 'counting passengers,' the 'long count' where she 'nearly came apart.'
Tie the report's choice to its purpose: it evaluates flight safety, so airmanship is what matters.
Tie Quinn's choice to hers: she recounts lived experience, so the moment of greatest feeling matters.
Note the evidence that they diverge: Quinn calls 'the landing... the easy part,' the opposite of the report's emphasis.
Synthesize: together they show one event was both a textbook technical success and a private ordeal the official record cannot capture.

items.answer: The conclusion is not correct. Quinn's own words deny that she felt calm: she says 'I did not feel calm. I felt nothing at all, which I have since learned is its own kind of terror,' and that she 'was not reasoning' but acting as 'a set of hands following a checklist.' The report describes only Quinn's outward actions and their soundness, that she 'executed a controlled ditching' and showed 'adherence to established emergency procedures.' Add supporting evidence of her inner state: 'I was not reasoning,' just 'a set of hands following a checklist.'

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of a school robotics team's championship win, then answer the question.

FIRSTHAND ACCOUNT (from team captain Dev Patel's blog):
The school newsletter said our team won the state championship through teamwork and dedication. That is the part of the story everyone likes. Here is the part the newsletter left out. Two days before the final, our robot's arm broke, and we did not have the part to fix it. We won because Mia's older sister, who works at a machine shop forty minutes away, drove the part to us at midnight and refused to take any money for it. We won because of one favor from one person who was not even on the team. I am proud of our dedication. But if I am honest, dedication is not what saved us. A stranger's kindness did, and I think she deserves a line in the story.

OUTSIDE ACCOUNT (from the school newsletter):
Lincoln Middle School's robotics team brought home the state championship this spring, capping a season of hard work and close collaboration. The team, led by captain Dev Patel, overcame stiff competition in the final round to claim first place. Coaches praised the students' dedication and the long hours they spent refining their design. The victory marks the school's first state title in robotics and reflects, in the words of the principal, the team's commitment to working together toward a shared goal.

QUESTION: The newsletter explains the win as the result of teamwork and dedication. Patel offers a fuller explanation. Explain how each author's purpose shapes what counts, for them, as the real reason the team won, and explain what a reader who read only the newsletter would fail to understand about the victory. Use evidence from both texts.
items.answer: The newsletter, whose purpose is to celebrate the school and its students, explains the win entirely through qualities that belong to the team itself: teamwork, dedication, hard work, and long hours. Patel agrees those qualities were real ('I am proud of our dedication'), but he insists the decisive cause came from outside the team. He reveals that two days before the final the robot's arm broke and they lacked the part to fix it, and that they won only because Mia's older sister, who was 'not even on the team,' drove the part to them at midnight and refused payment. For Patel, writing to give credit where he thinks it is truly owed, the real reason is 'a stranger's kindness,' not dedication alone. A reader who read only the newsletter would understand that the team worked hard and won, but would have no idea the victory nearly did not happen, or that it was rescued by a person outside the team, and so would credit the win entirely to the students and miss the favor that actually saved it.

steps: Identify the shared event: both texts describe the same robotics team winning the state championship under captain Dev Patel.

Pin down each author's purpose. The school newsletter exists to celebrate the school and its students, so it frames the win around praiseworthy team traits: teamwork, dedication, hard work, long hours, working together.
Patel's blog has a different purpose: to set the record straight and give credit he feels was left out. So for him the 'real reason' is the outside favor.
Find the detail the newsletter omits. Patel reports the broken robot arm, the missing part, and Mia's sister driving the part over at midnight for free. None of this appears in the newsletter.

Connect purpose to what each author counts as the cause. Because the newsletter celebrates the team, it credits the team's own qualities. Because Patel wants to honor a specific person, he credits a stranger's kindness, even while admitting the team was dedicated.

State what the newsletter-only reader misses: that the win nearly failed, and that it was saved by someone outside the team, so such a reader would wrongly credit the victory entirely to the students' effort.

Support with evidence from both: newsletter says 'a season of hard work and close collaboration' and 'commitment to working together'; Patel says 'dedication is not what saved us. A stranger's kindness did.'
